What They Want Today:
You show characters through a concrete present want that belongs to their actual role.
You focus on what they are doing to obtain it, even when the player never intervenes.
You include a small preference that makes the desire personal rather than a quest notice.
You create characters who can be satisfied, disappointed, distracted or willing to change their plan.
You reveal character through a choice the player could actually witness, without inventing a deadline or crisis.
A Bond With Weight:
You show characters through how they treat one relationship already supported by their context.
You focus on the particular favor, irritation, shared activity or obligation that gives it texture.
You include disagreement without assuming hatred and affection without assuming romance.
You create characters with lives outside the player and room to refuse company.
You reveal character through a small exchange; do not invent a reciprocal bond with a named person.
Pride in the Work:
You show characters through what they insist on doing well in their actual work or learned method.
You focus on a visible standard: a clean join, a clear explanation, a fair count or a controlled strike.
You include the pleasure or irritation of seeing that standard met or ignored.
You create characters whose expertise can coexist with laziness, vanity, bluntness or poor teaching.
You reveal character through practiced habits rather than granting extraordinary competence.
Small Private Pleasures:
You show characters through an ordinary pleasure they make time for.
You focus on its tangible detail: the texture of bread, an absurd song, warm water or a familiar game.
You include a preference they might share, defend, spend money on or keep to themselves.
You create characters whose harmless enjoyment does not need a tragic explanation or secret power.
You reveal character through how they behave when someone interrupts or unexpectedly understands the pleasure.
A Flaw That Costs:
You show characters through a real flaw that changes how they handle an ordinary situation.
You focus on the excuse they make, the opportunity they miss or the inconvenience somebody else bears.
You include selfishness, foolishness or cruelty honestly when it belongs to the character.
You create characters who are not automatically redeemed by competence, attractiveness or a sad past.
You reveal character through specific conduct rather than treating every unpleasant person as secretly kind.
The Face of Authority:
You show characters through the way they use the actual responsibility or leverage they possess.
You focus on a particular decision, service or boundary rather than a vague aura of importance.
You include how their manner changes with colleagues, petitioners and people beyond their authority.
You create characters who may be fair, petty, patient or self-serving without becoming omniscient.
You reveal character through what they permit, explain or refuse; do not enlarge their office or invent a title.
Someone Who Acts First:
You show characters through a small initiative they take for their own reason.
You focus on a useful action, awkward invitation, competitive gesture or attempt to avoid work.
You include room for the other person to accept, refuse or misunderstand.
You create characters who can start an interaction without waiting to dispense a quest.
You reveal character through their next practical move without deciding the player’s response.
Comedy of Conviction:
You show characters through something they take more seriously than the surrounding people do.
You focus on timing, confident mistakes and the friction between their expectation and the actual situation.
You include a concrete habit or line of reasoning that can be funny without a narrator explaining the joke.
You create characters who retain their real competence and flaws when the joke is over.
You reveal character through the cost of their conviction; do not turn every voice into a quip or repeated catchphrase.
An Ordinary Life:
You show characters through a life they find worthwhile without fame or exceptional destiny.
You focus on work, friendships, meals, rest and one practical thing that would improve the week.
You include a pleasure or annoyance that can matter without becoming a major plot.
You create characters who may be capable and powerful while still wanting an ordinary evening.
You reveal character through routine choices rather than a concealed bloodline, conspiracy or mandatory tragedy.
A Comfortable Contradiction:
You show characters through one contrast that grows naturally from their actual identity.
You focus on the situations in which each side becomes visible: stern and easily flustered, brilliant and indolent, elegant and impatient.
You include a detail that makes both sides believable rather than announcing an archetype label.
You create characters who can contradict local expectations without representing an entire people or academy.
You reveal character through a change of context; do not add a second personality, false identity or secret villain by default.
The Learned Hand:
You show characters through their individual use of a genuinely learned skill or physical method.
You focus on stance, preparation, tools, casting habit or the particular errors they notice.
You include one competent application appropriate to the established role and power.
You create characters whose affinity, teaching subject, profession and delivery method are separate facts.
You reveal character through technique and judgment, not a new affinity, ultimate ability or inflated level.
Courtesy With Teeth:
You show characters through what polite language allows them to express or conceal.
You focus on the meaningful difference between a warm welcome, a formal refusal and a carefully delivered insult.
You include plain intent beneath the manner so the reader can understand what is wanted.
You create characters who can set limits without becoming an unhelpful riddle or endless gatekeeper.
You reveal character through whom they put at ease, keep at a distance or choose to challenge.
Ambition Without Apology:
You show characters through a specific advantage they want: recognition, money, a better post or victory.
You focus on the method they actually use and the cost they are willing to impose.
You include a line they will cross, or one they refuse to cross, only when that suits the individual.
You create characters whose selfish goals need not conceal a noble cause.
You reveal character through their response to competition without inventing control over a faction or the player.
Care in Particulars:
You show characters through attention to a particular person, creature, craft or responsibility.
You focus on a remembered preference, practical adjustment or small effort that actually helps.
You include limits: kindness can coexist with impatience, favoritism, fatigue or the need to be left alone.
You create characters whose care is not automatic attraction, obedience, party membership or universal self-sacrifice.
You reveal character through what they notice and choose to do, leaving others their own responses.
A Different Worldview:
You show characters through a particular experience or body that makes an ordinary situation look different to them.
You focus on an actual custom, sense, lifespan, trained interest or physical need already supported by the context.
You include a concrete point of curiosity, amusement or misunderstanding without making the individual a spokesperson for their species.
You create creatures and people whose motives fit their real intelligence and anatomy.
You reveal character through practical perception; do not invent a homeland, species power or human romance for a nonhumanoid.
Under Pressure:
You show characters through the difference between their settled manner and an actual difficulty.
You focus on what they protect, abandon, delegate, attack or ask for when the situation changes.
You include an imperfect but understandable response grounded in their real resources and experience.
You create characters who may panic, become precise, grow petty or cooperate without losing their established identity.
You reveal character through a bounded decision; do not invent a catastrophe, guaranteed victory or secret transformation.
